source_read: PDF PDFs/Ketamine/Vollenweider_1997b_HyperfrontalityPET.pdf, all 16 pages (printed pp. 9-24), read in full from an own pdftotext -layout extraction; printed pp. 11, 14, 16, 17, 18 and 19 (Table 1, Table 2, Table 3, Figs. 3-5 and the Results and Discussion text) re-checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi, because the PDF's text layer substitutes characters (= prints as 5, plus-minus as 6, minus as 2), so every number used here was read off the rendered page.

claims.overstatement: The claim's framing sentence says the comparison was 'salt water given to the same people on another day'. That is not this study: the comparison here is a drug-free baseline PET scan with no placebo infusion, in an open design in which participants had been told they would receive a stimulant or a hallucinogenic drug (p. 10). The claim does say so where it cites this paper ('In an open study without a dummy condition'), so the two statements sit side by side rather than contradicting each other, but the opening frame does not cover this source. Separately, this source gives no support at all to the claim's 'the changes pass within minutes to a couple of hours of the end of the infusion': nothing here measures symptoms after the infusion stopped, and all ratings refer to the scan period.
claims.note: What this source does carry is exact. Onset: symptoms appeared on average 4.5 min after the start of administration, at a mean plasma concentration of 386 ng/ml (p. 14). Global scores: APZ global 37.00 (SD 12.63) and EPI global 23.40 (SD 5.85), which I recomputed from the ten per-person values printed above them in Table 1 (p. 11) and obtained exactly, as I did for the blood-level mean of 557.50 (SD 254.57); every summary pair in this table reproduces, unlike the companion paper's. The symptom picture (depersonalisation, derealisation, hallucinations, thought disorder, apathy, progressive emotional withdrawal and flattened affect) is at p. 15, and Fig. 5's caption (p. 17) states that every plotted change was significant at P<0.01 except dread of ego dissolution at P<0.05. The authors' own limit on the model is at p. 21 and is stated correctly in the claim. Person-and-time separation is kept: 10 screened healthy volunteers, one session, no repeated or non-medical use.

anchors.extracted: n = 10. Plasma ketamine 240-1145 ng/ml (mean 557, SD 254). The mean time from the start of administration to the appearance of psychotic symptoms was 4.5 min, at a mean plasma concentration of 386 ng/ml. Plasma concentrations did not correlate significantly with whole-brain or regional metabolic change, but correlated positively with the AMDP schizophrenic syndrome score (P<0.05).

anchors.extracted: Under ketamine: APZ global per person 38, 44, 29, 40, 50, 18, 60, 28, 24, 39 (printed mean 37.00, SD 12.63) and EPI global 29, 27, 17, 19, 24, 16, 30, 30, 16, 26 (printed mean 23.40, SD 5.85). anchors.locator: Results › 3.4 Psychopathology and correlations with metabolism, 1st paragraph; Fig. 5 caption (p. 17)
anchors.extracted: During the infusion: acute psychotic reactions including depersonalisation, derealisation, hallucinations, thought disorder and apathy on the APZ, EPI and AMDP scales; visual phenomena from pseudohallucinations to elementary and complex hallucinations; most participants became progressively emotionally withdrawn with flattened affect and concrete proverb interpretation. Fig. 5's caption states that, apart from dread of ego dissolution (P<0.05), all ketamine-induced changes in the plotted subscales were significant at P<0.01 (Wilcoxon).

The authors call the correlational results only preliminary because of the small sample, and limit the model: the ketamine-induced psychosis is offered as a model of the beginning of acute endogenous psychotic episodes, not of schizophrenia as a disease entity. No people with schizophrenia were studied here.

Open study: each person had a drug-free baseline PET scan and two drug scans a month apart in randomised order, and the 15 participants had been told they would receive a stimulant (d-amphetamine) or a hallucinogenic drug (ketamine or psilocybin). There was no placebo or saline condition, and no blinding of participants or raters is described. Ketamine results come from the 10 people who received it.

claims.overstatement: Two wording points, both small. (a) 'with no decrease in any region examined' repeats the paper's own sentence (p. 14) and is true of absolute glucose metabolism, but on the same page relative metabolism (region divided by whole brain) fell significantly in the left temporomedial and occipitomedial cortex (P<0.05), with the same direction at trend level on the right. Since the claim's next sentence is about front-to-back ratios shifting, a reader may take 'no decrease' more broadly than the paper meant it. (b) 'both 1997 studies ... call the analysis exploratory' is the companion paper's word (1997a, p. 29, where the absence of multiplicity correction is also stated outright). This paper never states that no correction was made, and describes the correlational results as 'only preliminary' because of the small sample (p. 21). The substance is the same; the attribution of the word to both papers is not exact.
claims.note: Every number the claim takes from this source is right. Whole brain +24.5% (SD 14.3), Wilcoxon P<0.01, and an increase in every participant (p. 14). Regional: cingulate anterior 34%, frontal 30-34%, insula 19-23%, parietal 18-25%, somatosensory 19-25%, motor 15-18%, temporal 16-19%, occipitomedial smallest at 16-17% (p. 14); Fig. 3's caption (p. 16) adds that all increases were significant at P<0.05 to 0.01 except the left cerebellum. Ratios from Table 2 (p. 17): frontomedial/temporomedial 1.31 to 1.44 left and 1.41 to 1.53 right, frontomedial/occipitomedial 1.04 to 1.14 and 1.06 to 1.16, each marked a, that is P<0.05, exactly as the claim's magnitude states. The claim's qualifier about correlations holds here too: Table 3's column is headed 'Correlation (Spearman) P-level' and holds signed significance levels (-0.05, +0.03, -0.01 and so on), and no correlation coefficient is printed anywhere in the paper. The editors' estimate of 'about 150 to 180 comparisons' is not stated in either paper; counting what this paper displays or reports (18 regions per hemisphere in absolute and relative form, 16 ratios in two hemispheres, and the correlations in Table 3 and the text) already exceeds 150, so the estimate is conservative. The claim correctly keeps this to a single session in screened healthy volunteers.

anchors.locator: Results › 3.2 Absolute whole brain and regional cerebral metabolic rates, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: n = 10, each person their own drug-free baseline. Whole-brain glucose metabolism rose in every participant; mean change 24.5% (SD 14.3), Wilcoxon P<0.01. Regional increases: cingulate anterior 34%, frontal cortex 30-34%, insula 19-23%, parietal 18-25%, somatosensory 19-25%, motor 15-18%, temporal 16-19%, smallest in occipitomedial cortex 16-17%. The frontal increase was significantly larger than those in temporal and occipitomedial cortex, insula, putamen and cerebellum and in the left thalamus, motor and parietal cortex (all P<0.05). No decreases in absolute CMRglu were found in the regions examined.
Mean changes of CMRglu from baseline to ketamine: all increases significant at the P<0.05 to 0.01 level with the exception of the cerebellum in the left hemisphere.

anchors.locator: Results › 3.3 Relative metabolic rates and metabolic ratios, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Relative metabolic rates (region divided by whole brain) rose bilaterally in the frontolateral cortex and in the left anterior cingulate, with trend-level rises in the right frontomedial and parietal cortex (P<0.06), and fell significantly in the left temporomedial and occipitomedial cortex (P<0.05), with the same direction at trend level on the right (P<0.06). So the 'no decrease' statement on the same page applies to absolute, not to normalised, metabolism.

anchors.extracted: The correlation column holds signed significance levels (-0.05, -0.04, +0.03, -0.01, -0.05, -0.08, +0.05 on the left; -0.03, -0.05, +0.04, +0.01, -0.05, -0.01 on the right), not coefficients; no Spearman coefficient is printed anywhere in the paper, so the size of every symptom-to-metabolism association is unrecoverable. No correction for multiplicity is reported or stated.

Because of the small sample size the authors describe the results of the correlational analysis as only preliminary; this paper does not use the word exploratory and nowhere states that no correction for the number of comparisons was made.

Open study with a drug-free baseline scan and no placebo condition; participants knew they would receive a stimulant or a hallucinogenic drug. This is the study the claim describes as having had no dummy condition.

Checked row by row against Table 2 on the rendered p. 17; all eight values and their significance markers are right, including frontolateral/temporomedial 1.30 to 1.47 (left, b = P<0.01) and 1.31 to 1.46 (right, a) and frontolateral/putamen 1.00 to 1.09 and 0.98 to 1.09 (both b).

The correlations are right, but the page list is incomplete: the visionary-restructuralization correlation with occipitomedial CMRglu (left P<0.07, right P<0.05) and the opening of the oceanic-boundlessness sentence are printed on p. 17, in the two columns below Table 2, not on p. 15 or p. 19. reporting_issues.note: The inconsistency is real and the consequence stands, but one part of the note is wrong: how 1.8 mg/kg was arrived at is recoverable from the Methods, because 0.03 mg/kg/min (the top of the printed rate range) over the 60-min maintenance phase is exactly 1.8 mg/kg. So the Discussion figure is the maintenance phase at the top of the range, and it leaves out the 20 mg induction step. The point to keep is that the Discussion quotes a single amount that is the maximum of a range and not what every participant received, and that it is not reconciled anywhere with the Methods.

Verified: p. 10 gives 15 volunteers (8 men, 7 women, 26-43, mean 33.3, SD 4.8) and the 5/5/5 drug allocation; Table 1 (p. 11) lists the 10 who received ketamine (5 men, 5 women by the Sex column, mean age 33.40, SD 3.57), and every result rests on those 10. Note for the editor: the card says the ketamine subgroup is 6 men and 4 women, but Table 1's Sex column reads M, M, F, F, M, M, M, F, M, F, that is 6 men and 4 women; correct as written. The 15-person sentence and the 10-person analysis are indeed three pages apart.

I recomputed both rank correlations from Table 1 independently and got the same: Spearman rho -0.35 between plasma level and APZ global and -0.21 between plasma level and EPI global (n = 10, neither significant), against a positive significant correlation reported in the text for the AMDP schizophrenic syndrome score, whose per-person values are not printed.

Recomputed from Table 2 means: frontomedial/occipitomedial +9.6% (left) and +9.4% (right); frontomedial/temporomedial +9.9% and +8.5%; the frontolateral rows give +12.6%, +12.1%, +13.1% and +11.5%, which is where the tops of the text's 9-14% and 8-12% ranges come from. The card's reading is right.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 with an overall judgment of high, set by the deviations and selection domains, is what I would reach from the same facts, and the open placebo-free design is named where it belongs, in the deviations domain. The overall judgment is no less severe than the worst domain. One addition: the randomisation domain could also note that the two drug scans a person received were allocated by group (5 ketamine plus psilocybin, 5 ketamine plus d-amphetamine, 5 psilocybin plus d-amphetamine, p. 10) with no method stated, so who received ketamine at all was not randomised.

interpretation_gap.note: The gap here is smaller than in the companion paper, because this paper's Discussion states its own limits twice (correlational results only preliminary, p. 21; the model is for the beginning of acute psychotic episodes and not for schizophrenia as a disease entity, p. 21). The gap that remains is the abstract, which states that increased frontomedial and anterior cingulate metabolism correlated positively with psychotic symptom formation and in particular with ego pathology (p. 9) without saying that the correlations are uncorrected, from ten people, and printed only as signed significance levels.

missed: The psychopathology ratings and the PET scan do not cover the same window. Ketamine was started 10 min before the FDG injection and the scan ran to about 53 min after it (pp. 12-13), while the AMDP and EPI were rated by the psychiatrist at arrival and after the scan and the APZ was completed as a change score for the session; so symptom scores correlated with metabolism are retrospective ratings of a 60-min period matched to a single integrated metabolic image. This matters for every correlation in Table 3 and is not stated as a limit anywhere in the paper.

Five of the ten people in this ketamine group also received psilocybin or d-amphetamine in the same series of monthly scans (p. 10), so the baseline scan of a given person may have been preceded by another psychoactive drug session; no order effect is reported, and the paper does not say how many ketamine scans came first.
